title.en: Degree modifiers: quite, rather, fairly, absolutely
title.es: Modificadores de grado: quite, rather, fairly, absolutely

summary.en: Modifiers change how strong an adjective or adverb is. **Gradable** adjectives (_good, tired, cold, expensive_) accept _very, extremely, really, fairly, quite, pretty, rather, slightly, a bit_. **Extreme or ungradable** adjectives (_fantastic, exhausted, freezing, impossible, perfect_) do not take _very_; use _absolutely, completely, utterly, totally_ or _really_. **Quite** is tricky: with gradable words it means 'to a moderate degree' in British English (_quite good_), but with extreme words it means 'completely' (_quite impossible_). _Rather_ often suggests more than expected or something negative (_rather expensive_), and _pretty_ is informal. For comparatives use _much, far, a lot, slightly, a bit_, never _very_. These choices make your tone precise, which matters in Speaking part 4 and in formal writing.
summary.es: **Very** solo con adjetivos graduables; con los extremos (agotado, helado, imposible) usa absolutely o completely. Para comparativos usa much / far, no *very better*. Ojo: quite no es «quitar», sino «bastante» o «del todo».

form: Gradable adjective: **fairly / quite / pretty / rather / very / extremely + adjective**
Extreme adjective: **absolutely / completely / utterly / totally / really + adjective**
Comparatives: **much / far / a lot / slightly / a bit + comparative** (_much cheaper_)
Too: **far / much too + adjective** (not _too much_ before an adjective)
Word order with nouns: **quite a** / **rather a** + adjective + noun, or **a** + **quite / rather** + adjective + noun (_quite a nice day_, _a rather nice day_)
Informal: _pretty good_, _a bit tired_; formal: _somewhat disappointed_, _rather concerned_

uses.text: **Moderate degree** → _The hotel was fairly cheap, but quite far from the centre._
**Strong feeling with extreme adjectives** → _The view from the top was absolutely breathtaking._
**Complaining politely** → _I was rather disappointed with the service._

note.en: Rather and somewhat soften a complaint in a formal email while still making it clear.
note.es: Rather y somewhat suavizan una queja en un correo formal.

uses.text: **Comparing** → _My new flat is much bigger than the old one._
**Quite a + noun** → _That was quite a surprise._ (meaning a big surprise)

mistakes.wrong: The view from the top was very magnificent.
mistakes.right: The view from the top was absolutely magnificent.

why.en: Magnificent is already extreme, so use absolutely or really, not very.
why.es: Magnificent ya es extremo: absolutely o really, no very.

mistakes.wrong: My new job is very better than the old one.
mistakes.right: My new job is much better than the old one.

why.en: Very does not modify comparatives; use much, far or a lot.
why.es: Muy mejor se dice much better.

why.en: With a noun alone, the order is quite a + noun.
why.es: Sin adjetivo, el orden es quite a + sustantivo.

examples.en: The film was fairly entertaining, but it went on a bit too long.
It was absolutely freezing in the tent, so nobody slept.
examples.es: Hacía un frío helador en la tienda, así que nadie durmió.

examples.en: I thought the exam was quite difficult, but most students passed.
It is quite impossible to park here on Saturdays.
examples.es: Es del todo imposible aparcar aquí los sábados.

examples.en: We were rather surprised to hear the price had doubled.
The new menu is a lot cheaper than the old one.
That was quite a surprise; nobody expected her to resign.
He was completely exhausted after the long journey.
The rucksack is far too heavy for a child to carry.
I'm pretty tired, so I think I'll go to bed early.
We were somewhat disappointed with the quality of the room.

practice.prompt: It's ___ impossible to park here on Saturdays.

explanation.en: Impossible is an extreme adjective, so it takes absolutely.

practice.prompt: My new flat is ___ bigger than the old one.

explanation.en: Comparatives take much, far or a lot, not very or quite.

practice.prompt: That was ___ surprise: nobody expected her to resign.

explanation.en: The order is quite a + noun.

practice.prompt: The rucksack is ___ heavy for a child to carry.

explanation.en: Use far too (or much too) before an adjective; too much goes before nouns.
